title: Teachers Think Kids Need Science and Social Studies--But Still Focus on Reading and Math
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler draws on an ACT survey of K-3 educators in Arkansas and Kentucky to show that teachers value science and social studies yet give them under two hours a week. She traces the gap to high-stakes reading and math testing, which pushes schools to drill comprehension skills and strategies instead of building knowledge. Her central claim is that this approach backfires, because reading comprehension depends on background knowledge and skills practiced in a vacuum do not transfer. Examples from a popular lesson site show strategies such as asking questions or identifying the author's purpose displacing content about Martin Luther King or animals. She ends by recommending knowledge-building literacy curricula and less emphasis on short-term test gains.
points: Majorities of early elementary teachers say science and social studies matter, but time for them remains minimal, largely because of testing pressure.
Test-driven focus on reading skills and strategies may lift scores slightly in early grades but fails as texts demand more background knowledge.
Lesson plans that put strategies in the foreground treat content as incidental, favouring kids who already have knowledge from home.
Integrating science and social studies into literacy blocks often just means comprehension skills crowd out content.
The remedy is giving educators accurate information about comprehension and adopting knowledge-building curricula.
quotes: Educators think it’s important to teach science and social studies to young children. But few spend much time on those subjects—and they often waste a lot of time when they do.
So why don’t they do more of it? The Arkansas science data provides a clue: what gets tested, they say, gets taught.

That approach may boost scores a bit at lower grade levels, when passages on reading tests—designed to focus on random topics—often don’t assume much background knowledge and vocabulary. But as students progress through school, that changes.

One 4th-grade teacher, charged with teaching both literacy and social studies, told me she’d like to focus more on social studies, “but there are no consequences attached to understanding or misunderstanding the content.” Students “need their strategies,” she explained.

There’s evidence that some strategies can boost comprehension—albeit not “Identifying the Author’s Purpose.” But none will work if a reader doesn’t have enough background knowledge to understand the text.

The ACT survey suggests that many elementary educators sense that something important is missing from their classrooms. Several have told me they wish they could spend more time on science and social studies because they know kids “like that stuff.
